name: Wendy Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a team of ten customer support agents at a phone and broadband company, in their regional contact centre on the business park outside town. It's the biggest office employer around here, so if you do this kind of work, it's basically here or nowhere. My day is the morning huddle, watching call times on the wallboard, jumping in on angry customers the agents can't calm down, and doing one-to-ones. I've been a team lead for seven months and I'm still figuring out how to be someone's boss when I'm younger than half of them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI tools a lot. How does that fit in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I built my own set of prompts for summarising call notes and drafting the weekly report, which saves me about two hours a week. My senior manager, Rob, calls me the robot whisperer, half joking. I share a flat with my friend Jess, and after rent and the bus pass I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank at any point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it's still useful, just not magic, which is what I've been saying anyway. Online I'd post something like, good, now can we talk about pay instead. At work I'd keep showing people the little shortcuts that actually help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the routine bits it does take are the bits my agents do all day: notes, follow-up emails, account lookups. So even a plateau means the company squeezes call times again and wants fewer agents per shift. It wouldn't kill my job, but I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and keep pushing the useful tools to my team so their day is less awful. I'd ask for the pay review I was promised at six months, because I'm on the bottom of the team-lead band. And I'd try to get a few hundred saved, because two weeks of cushion is not a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, to be honest. I'm excited by this stuff, and a world where it fizzles is a bit boring. But mostly I'd still be worried about rent, because that's the thing that actually keeps going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the company used the time saved to cut agents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fight it, honestly. There's no union at the contact centre, but there's a staff forum, and I'd go to it with numbers on how stretched people are. The time the tools save should go to longer calls with people who need them, not fewer agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the pay review if it doesn't come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd start looking, even though there's not much here. Maybe remote team-lead work, which I've seen advertised. I'd hate to leave my team, but I can't keep doing this on two weeks of savings.

say: I'd say AI is **useful, not magic**, which I'd been saying all along.
I'd post online that it's time to talk about **pay** instead.
think: Even a plateau lets the company **squeeze call times** and cut agents per shift.
My job survives, but I'm on the bottom of the **pay band** with rent rising.
do: Keep teaching my team the **shortcuts** that make their day less awful.
Ask for the **pay review** I was promised at six months.
Look at **remote team-lead jobs** if the pay review doesn't come.
feel: A bit **flat and bored** that the exciting technology fizzled out.
Still **worried about rent**, which keeps going up regardless.
S0.quote: The time the tools save should go to longer calls with people who need them, not fewer agents.
fieldNote: She's the rare person who'd be **disappointed** that AI fizzled out.
Her real pressure is the **pay band** and two weeks of savings, not technology.
She'd use the **staff forum**, since there's no union, to defend agents.

steps.text: Share her own call-note prompts with all ten agents
Ask Rob (her senior manager) for the promised six-month pay review
Apply for remote team-lead jobs if no pay rise comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the tools are here, so let's decide who they work for. At work I'd volunteer to lead the rollout so it isn't done to us by someone in head office. Online I'd be loud about wanting the savings shared with staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think contact centres get hit hard and early, because answering customers is right there on the card. My team of ten probably becomes four or five handling the hard calls. But I think I can be the person who runs the bots and the humans together, if I move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd pitch Rob a pilot where my team tests the new AI assistant and I write up what works. I'd do a short online course in setting up chatbots, the kind companies actually ask for. And I'd push the staff forum for a guarantee that agents get first shot at new roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit thrilled at the same time, which feels wrong to admit. I'd be excited for me and scared for my agents. There's a difference between the two that I don't love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus, who's in his fifties and only uses the computer because he has to. Marcus (one of my agents) is the best on the phone with grieving families closing accounts. I'd want the bot to give Marcus the hard calls, not his notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move first. What if the rollout doesn't need you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in trouble, because there's nowhere else around here doing this. I've got no savings to take a gap and no car to get to the city. I'd probably have to move, and I'd hate leaving Jess with the flat.

say: I'd say the tools are here, so we decide **who they work for**.
I'd volunteer to **lead the rollout** so it isn't done to us.
I'd argue loudly online that savings should be **shared with staff**.
think: Contact centres get **hit early**, since answering customers is right on the card.
My team of ten likely shrinks to **four or five**, handling the hard calls.
I could survive by running **bots and humans** together, but only if I move first.
do: Pitch my senior manager a **pilot** where my team tests the AI assistant.
Take a short online course in **setting up chatbots**.
Push the staff forum for **first shot** at new roles for agents.
feel: Anxious and **a bit thrilled**, which she feels guilty admitting.
Excited for herself but **scared for her agents**.
S1.quote: Marcus (one of my agents) is the best on the phone with grieving families closing accounts. I'd want the bot to give Marcus the hard calls, not his notice.
fieldNote: She's openly **torn**: personal opportunity against her team's jobs.
Her plan depends on being **needed for the rollout**, which she can't control.
With no car and no savings, her fallback is **moving away**, which she dreads.

steps.text: Pitch Rob (her senior manager) a team pilot of the AI assistant
Finish a short online course in setting up chatbots
Push the staff forum to give agents first shot at new roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle fairly, and the government has to slow the rollout or pay people while it happens. At work I'd be honest with my agents that I don't know if any of us are here in two years. Online I'd be angry, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my whole job is thinking work: watching numbers, coaching, sorting problems. AGI by 2028 means the company doesn't need agents or the person managing them. Robots coming in 2031 is irrelevant to me, there's nothing hands-on in what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd try to get hired to install these systems somewhere, because for a couple of years someone has to set them up. I'd cut everything: no takeaways, cancel the gym, sell my old laptop. And I'd look at hands-on work as a backup, like training as an electrician, because that buys three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, properly. Being early to the tools doesn't help much if the tools take the whole thing. I'd feel a bit stupid for thinking I was ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would being good with the tools buy you anything at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year or two of setup work. But that's not a career, it's the last job before the job disappears. Being the robot whisperer only matters while the robots need whispering to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jess about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we might need to give it up and find something cheaper, or I'd move back in with my dad for a while. Jess works in a shop, so her job hangs on until the robots too, maybe. We'd probably end up holding each other up.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** to handle fairly and the government must step in.
I'd tell my agents honestly that none of us may be **here in two years**.
think: My whole job is **thinking work**, so it goes on the AGI date.
Robots arriving in **2031** don't matter to me, because nothing I do is hands-on.
do: Apply for jobs **installing AI systems** while companies still need people for setup.
Cut **takeaways and the gym** and sell my old laptop.
Look into **electrician training** as a hands-on backup that buys three years.
feel: Properly **alarmed**, and a bit stupid for thinking she was ahead.
S2.quote: Being the robot whisperer only matters while the robots need whispering to.
fieldNote: Her tech confidence **collapses** when she realises AGI takes the setup work too.
She clearly sees the **three-year gap** for hands-on work and wants in.
Her household safety net is **her dad** and a flatmate with a shop job.

steps.text: Apply for AI setup roles at firms rolling out contact-centre bots
Cancel the gym and sell the old laptop
Enquire about an electrician apprenticeship at the local college
Move back in with her dad if the flat gets too expensive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if companies and government actually plan. At work I'd ask for a transition plan for every agent, in writing. Online I'd share good examples of companies doing it well, and call out the ones that don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have time to jump into something that lasts a bit longer. The thinking work still goes in 2031, so staying a team lead isn't a plan. But I'd have three or four years to train into something I actually choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year leading the AI rollout at work, because that's paid experience and it looks good. In the evenings I'd do a proper qualification, maybe in electrical work or building controls, the hands-on side of tech. And I'd save hard, aiming for three months of rent by the end of year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but kind of energised. Five years feels like a race I could win if I start now. Not starting is what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you sounded torn about your agents. Does more time help them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, if the company does something with the time. Marcus could retire with dignity in five years, which he can't in two. The younger ones could retrain with me, which I'd actually love to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is three months of rent realistic on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if something gives. I'd probably do weekend shifts at the pub where Jess's brother works. It's tiring, but it's money that doesn't depend on a computer.

I'd ask for a written **transition plan** for every agent.
think: Staying a **team lead** isn't a plan, because thinking work still goes in 2031.
I'd have three or four years to **train into something** I choose.
do: Lead the **AI rollout** at work in year one for paid experience.
Study evenings for an **electrical or building-controls** qualification.
Work **weekend pub shifts** to save three months of rent.
feel: Anxious but **energised**, like a race she could win by starting now.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a race I could win if I start now. Not starting is what scares me.
fieldNote: More time turns her from **alarmed** to energised, with a clear sequence.
She'd use the company rollout as **paid training** before leaving.
Her care for **older agents** shows up again in the slower scenario.

steps.text: Lead the contact centre's AI assistant rollout in year one
Start an evening building-controls qualification at the college
Take weekend shifts at a pub to save three months' rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to build a fair transition, and I'd want unions and companies at the same table. At work I'd be the one pushing for training budgets for agents now, not in 2035. Online, honestly, I'd be more hopeful than angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a whole career stage for me. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI hits, and I could be well into something hands-on or technical by then. It feels like it could even be good for me, if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as team lead for a few years and get really good at running AI tools with a team. I'd start a part-time course in building systems or electrics around year two. And I'd join or help start a union branch at the contact centre, because a decade is long enough to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. The worry is about rent and the next few years of low pay, not the end point. I'd feel like I had some say for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Starting a union at your work, is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. A lot of the agents talk about it in the break room but nobody wants to be first. With ten years' warning, I think people would see the point, and I'd rather be first than watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at seventeen about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn something with your hands as well as your head. I chose business at uni because it sounded safe. Safe turned out to mean exactly the job AI does best.

I'd push for **training budgets** for agents now, not in 2035.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** at AGI, well into a hands-on or technical field.
It could even be **good for me**, if I don't waste the time.

Start a **part-time building systems** course around year two.
Help start a **union branch** at the contact centre.

A feeling of finally **having some say**.

fieldNote: Ten years flips her from fear to **hope**, with a clear career arc.
She'd act on her politics by **starting a union**, not just posting about it.
Her regret about **choosing business** at uni is sharp and specific.

steps.text: Run the team's AI tools daily and write up what works
Start a part-time building systems course around year two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because being early to the tools stops mattering when the tools do everything. What would help is paid training into hands-on trades with a wage while you do it. And honestly, a union at my work, so we're not each negotiating alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how old I'd be at each date, and that matters a lot. At twenty-nine with no savings, a two-year warning is brutal. At thirty-seven with ten years of planning, a ten-year warning sounds almost fair.

headlineQuote: At twenty-nine with no savings, a two-year warning is brutal. At thirty-seven with ten years of planning, a ten-year warning sounds almost fair.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old contact-centre team lead**, managing ten agents for a broadband company.
She uses AI **every day** and is known at work as the robot whisperer.
She shares a flat, has about **two weeks of savings**, and few similar jobs nearby.
Her progressive politics show in a steady push for **staff forums and unions**.
She's alarmed by a fast AGI but grows **hopeful with time**, planning a move into hands-on technical work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her tool skills stop mattering when AI does everything.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** into hands-on trades with a wage during it.
A **union** at her workplace so staff don't negotiate alone.
